extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in U.S. history, law, and free-speech issues
extracted.subtask_description: A short HISTORY.com article summarizing the 1988 U.S. Supreme Court decision overturning an award to Jerry Falwell and defending the right to satirize public figures under the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody falls within First Amendment protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Hustler's parody fell within the First Amendment’s protection of freedom of speech and the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court unanimously overturned the $200,000 settlement awarded to Reverend Jerry Falwell for emotional distress, ruling that the magazine's parody — though in poor taste — was protected speech. (Context: Hustler's 1983 parody of Falwell; decision in February 1988.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire of public figures is defensible even if offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive or tasteless parody of a public figure is nonetheless protected and cannot be the basis for the emotional-distress award upheld by lower courts in this case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that the Court viewed the parody as constitutionally protected despite its offensive nature; the 8-0 decision reversed the lower-court result after Falwell sued for libel and emotional distress.
